title: Arabic
font: "Noto Naskh Arabic", "Geeza Pro", "Segoe UI", Tahoma, serif
blurb: 28 letters written right to left, each with up to four joined forms.
writeTip: Arabic is written right to left. Most letters are written in one motion, with dots added after the body of the word.
notes: Arabic script (Modern Standard Arabic values) for SquirrelGo Alphabets. Letter forms are generated by the app with zero-width joiners. Hints, groupings and articles are original.

lessons.title: Alif and the boat family
lessons.note: ب ت ث ن ي share one boat-shaped body. Only the dots tell them apart.

chars.hint: alif: a long a; also carries hamza
bāʾ: b as in bed; one dot below
tāʾ: t; two dots above
thāʾ: th as in think; three dots above
nūn: n; one dot above, deeper bowl
yāʾ: y, or a long ee; two dots below
jīm: j as in jam; dot inside
ḥāʾ: a strong breathy h from the throat; no dot
khāʾ: ch as in Scottish loch; dot above

lessons.title: Letters that never join forward
lessons.note: These letters connect to the letter before them but always leave a gap after.

chars.hint: dāl: d
dhāl: th as in this
rāʾ: a tapped or rolled r
zāy: z
wāw: w, or a long oo

lessons.title: Teeth and loops
lessons.note: ص and ض are emphatic: said with the tongue root pulled back, which darkens nearby vowels.

chars.hint: sīn: s; three small teeth
shīn: sh; three dots above
ṣād: an emphatic, heavy s
ḍād: an emphatic, heavy d
ṭāʾ: an emphatic, heavy t
ẓāʾ: an emphatic, heavy th as in this
ʿayn: a voiced squeeze deep in the throat; no English match
ghayn: a gargled sound like a French r
fāʾ: f; one dot above
qāf: k from deep in the throat; two dots above
kāf: k as in kite
lām: l
mīm: m
hāʾ: a light h, as in hat

lessons.title: Extra letters and shapes
lessons.note: Not separate letters of the alphabet, but you will see them on every page.

chars.hint: hamza: a glottal stop, the catch in uh-oh
tāʾ marbūṭa: a feminine ending, said a (or at before another word)
alif maqṣūra: a long a at the end of a word, written like ي without dots
lām-alif: ل + ا always fuse into this shape

lessons.title: Short vowel marks
lessons.note: Short vowels are small marks above or below a letter. Adult texts usually leave them out; the Quran, children's books and dictionaries include them.

chars.hint: fatḥa: a short a, a stroke above
kasra: a short i, a stroke below
ḍamma: a short u, a small wāw above
sukūn: no vowel, a small circle above
shadda: the consonant is doubled
tanwīn: an -n ending on indefinite nouns

articles.title: Reading right to left
articles.body:
Arabic is written and read from right to left, and books open from what an English reader would call the back. Numbers are the exception: they are written left to right, even inside Arabic text.

The alphabet has 28 letters, all consonants. Three of them, ا, و and ي, also stand for the long vowels ā, ū and ī. Short vowels are optional marks above and below the letters.

Many letters share a basic shape and differ only in their dots, so the letters are taught here in shape families.

articles.title: Letters change shape
articles.body:
Arabic is always joined, in print as well as handwriting. Each letter has up to four forms depending on its position: alone, at the start of a word, in the middle, and at the end.

Take ب. Alone it is a full boat. At the start and in the middle it shrinks to a small tooth with its dot (بـ ـبـ). At the end the full boat comes back (ـب).

The word كتب (k-t-b) shows three forms in a row. Open the letter forms table to see every letter side by side.

articles.title: The six letters that don't join forward
articles.body:
ا د ذ ر ز و join to the letter before them but never to the letter after. Whatever follows them starts fresh, as if at the start of a word.

That is why a word like ورد (ward, rose) is written as three separate pieces, and why دار (dār, house) never joins up at all.

When you see a gap inside a word, the letter just before it is almost always one of these six.

articles.title: Sun and moon letters
articles.body:
The word for "the" is ال (al-), attached to the front of the noun. Before half of the alphabet, the l is swallowed and the next consonant is doubled instead:

الشمسash-shams, the sun, not al-shams
القمرal-qamar, the moon

The letters that absorb the l are the "sun letters", named after شمس: those made with the tongue tip, namely ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن. The rest are "moon letters". The l is still written either way.
